title: If only I had known: unreal conditions
title_target: Om jag hade vetat det, hade jag tagit med blommor i stället.
goal: Talk about what would have happened if things had gone differently — *om jag hade vetat…, skulle jag ha…* — drop the *om* the Swedish way, and express wishes and regrets with *önska att*.
bekal: you can build unreal past conditions with *om … hade* + supine and *skulle ha / hade* + supine
you can start a condition with the verb instead of *om*: *Hade jag vetat det…*
you can say *I wish…* with *önska att* and *in case* with *ifall*
wave: Go back to Unit 5: say its *skulle ha*, *borde ha* and *kunde ha* sentences aloud again, then add an *om*-clause in front of three of them (*Om jag hade läst mejlet, skulle jag ha vetat det*) — that is exactly the pattern of this unit.

notes: **Om jag hade tagit rätt spårvagn, skulle jag ha varit här…** — the unreal past condition. The *om*-clause takes **hade + supine** (*hade tagit*), the main clause takes **skulle ha + supine** (*skulle ha varit*). The logic is exactly English "If I had taken…, I would have been…". Never put *skulle* in the *om*-clause, though: *om jag skulle ha tagit* is a typical English-speaker mistake.

**Hade du ringt, kunde vi ha hämtat dig** — drop *om* and start with *hade*: ***Hade** du ringt…* = *Om du hade ringt…*. English can do this too ("Had you called…"), but there it sounds formal; in Swedish it's completely everyday. **Kunde ha** + supine means "could have".

**hade jag tagit med blommor** — in the main clause, spoken Swedish very often uses plain **hade** instead of *skulle ha*: *Om jag hade vetat det, **hade** jag tagit med blommor.* Both are correct; *hade… hade* is the more common one in conversation. Notice that the main clause still obeys V2: the verb comes straight after the *om*-clause.

**Och jag som just har bakat…** — *och jag som* + a clause expresses an ironic contrast: "and here I am, having just baked…". *Och jag som trodde att du var sjuk!* (And here I was, thinking you were ill!).

**blir det något över** — inverted conditions work for real conditions too: *Blir det något över…* = *Om det blir något över…* (If there's anything left over…). **Bli över** means "to be left over". **Ta med sig** (**tah MEHD say**) = to bring/take along: *ta med dig resten hem*.

**Hon hamnade i Angered** — *hamna* (**HAHM-nah**) means "to end up" somewhere you didn't plan to be. **Typ** (**tüp**), literally "type", is the spoken filler "like, sort of" — very common among younger Swedes. And **stan** is the everyday short form of *staden* (the town, downtown).

grammars.title: Three kinds of if
body: Swedish conditions line up neatly with English ones. The key is the verb in the *om*-clause: present for real, past for unreal now, *hade* + supine for unreal past.

head: Kind
Om-clause
Main clause
Example
rows: Om du **hade ringt**, **skulle** vi **ha hämtat** dig. / …**hade** vi **hämtat** dig.

after: All three can drop *om* and start with the verb: ***Ringer** du, hämtar vi dig.* — ***Ringde** du, skulle vi hämta dig.* — ***Hade** du ringt, hade vi hämtat dig.* The inverted version is especially common with *hade*.

The main clause can also start with **så** or **då**: *Om du hade ringt, **så** hade vi hämtat dig.* — *…**då** hade vi hämtat dig.* And it can stand alone when the condition is obvious: *Då hade jag kommit tidigare!* (Then I would have come earlier!)

dialogs.intro: Friday afternoon at the studio. Dian and Leila are tidying their desks before the weekend, and Leila is in a thoughtful mood.

lines.text: Jag önskar att jag hade gjort som du och pluggat utomlands.

notes: **Jag önskar att jag hade gjort…** — *önska att* + **hade + supine** expresses regret about the past: "I wish I had done…". For a wish about the present, use the plain **past**: *Jag önskar att jag **hade** mer tid* (I wish I had more time — here *hade* is just the past of *ha*), *Jag önskar att det inte **regnade***. In speech, *jag skulle önska att…* is a softer variant.

**Hade jag varit lite modigare, skulle jag kanske bo i Tokyo nu** — a **mixed** condition: the condition is in the past (*hade varit*), but the result is about now (*skulle bo… nu*). English does the same: "If I'd been braver, I'd be living in Tokyo now."

**Det hade varit synd** — "That would have been a shame." *Hade varit* on its own is the everyday way to say "would have been". In writing you'll also meet **vore** (**VOO-reh**), an old subjunctive meaning "would be": *Det vore synd*, *Om jag vore du…* (If I were you…). Recognize it; you'll use it actively in Svenska 104.

**de har lovat regn** — literally "they have promised rain": *lova* (**LOH-vah**) is the standard verb for weather forecasts. *De* here means the forecasters — usually **SMHI**, Sweden's weather service, whose app every Swede checks before going out.

**ifall det öser ner** — **ifall** (**ee-FAHL**) means "in case": *Ta med regnkläder ifall det regnar*. In speech it is also used simply as *om* ("if, whether"): *Jag undrar ifall hon kommer*. **Ösa ner** (**ö-sah NEHR**), "to bail down", is how Swedes say it's pouring.

**Det finns inget dåligt väder, bara dåliga kläder** — perhaps the most quoted Swedish proverb. You'll hear it from every Swedish parent sending children out into the rain — and from every Göteborger defending their city's weather.

grammars.title: Wishes and in-case: önska att, ifall
body: After *önska att*, Swedish shifts the verb **one step back in time**, just like English after "I wish".

head: What you mean
Swedish
English
rows: Jag önskar att jag **hade** mer tid.
I wish I had more time.
Jag önskar att jag **hade köpt** skor.
I wish I had bought shoes.
Jag hoppas att det **blir** sol i morgon.
I hope it'll be sunny tomorrow.
Bring rain gear in case it rains.

after: Don't use *önska* for realistic hopes about the future — that is **hoppas** (Svenska 102): *Jag hoppas att du kommer* (I hope you'll come). *Jag önskar att du kom* sounds like you know you won't.
*Önska* without *att* + noun means "to wish someone something": *Jag önskar dig en trevlig helg.* And remember that *att*-clauses follow BIFF: *Jag önskar att jag **inte** hade sagt det.*

blocks.text: The Swedish system is close to English, which is exactly why English speakers carry their habits over. These are the mistakes teachers correct most often at B1.

blocks.text: Being invited home for dinner is a sign of real friendship in Sweden, and there are a few unwritten rules. Arrive **on time** — not early, and not much later (if you're delayed, send a message). Take your **shoes off** in the hall; nobody walks around indoors in outdoor shoes. Bring something small: flowers, chocolates, or a bottle of wine if you know the hosts drink.

blocks.text: **Tack för senast** is the one foreigners forget. The next time you see your hosts — even weeks later — open with it. Forgetting it won't cause a scandal, but remembering it will make you sound like you grew up here.
